articles.title: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits Canada
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Canada this week for his first visit to the country in nearly a year as his country copes with an onslaught of deadly airstrikes.

image.caption: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a welcome ceremony at the Serbia Palace, in Belgrade in August. Zelenskyy is visiting Canada this week, the prime minister's office confirmed Wednesday. (Darko Vojinovic/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Canada this week for his first visit to the country in nearly a year as his country copes with an onslaught of deadly airstrikes.
Visit comes as Ukraine grapples with barrage of devastating air strikes
Zelenskyy will be in the country from Wednesday to Friday and attend events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay alongside his wife, Olena Zelenska, says a statement from Prime Minister Mark Carney.
"The visit underscores Canada's continued leadership in supporting Ukraine and reflects our unwavering commitment to a just and lasting peace," Carney said in the statement.
The visit will focus on "shared priorities" between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic and energy co-operation, Carney's statement said.
"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries."

The statement doesn't say when or where Zelenskyy is expected to arrive in Canada, but the prime minister's itinerary says he is meeting with Zelenskyy in Calgary on Thursday morning. The two leaders will participate in a signing ceremony and hold a news conference afterwards.

items: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expected to visit Canada next week: sources
Carney prepared to tell Putin to 'get out of Ukraine' if Russia welcomed to G20 summit

blocks.text: The Ukrainian president announced that he was travelling to Canada in a social media post on Wednesday, but did not say what city he was flying into.
Zelenskyy's most recent visit to Canada was last December, where he met with Carney in Halifax before travelling to the U.S. for talks focused on ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
Carney visited Kyiv last August in his first official visit to the country, where he reiterated Canada's support for Ukraine and unveiled details of an additional $2 billion in military aid.
Flight delayed Tuesday due to drone activity

On Tuesday, a flight scheduled to carry Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was ​delayed when authorities closed Moldova's airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.
Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries.

On Wednesday, government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova had closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon to protect aircraft flying over the country at the time, delaying three departures, including Zelenskyy's.
Zelenskyy's visit comes as Kyiv copes with devastating airstrikes and as his government pleads for more air defence support. European leaders argue Russia has been widening its war.
Intelligence warns Putin is preparing escalation in Ukraine
Before travelling to Canada, Zelenskky chided the international community for not taking a tougher stance against Russia over its escalating bombardment of civilian areas of Ukraine.
"Unfortunately, there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes, which are taking people's lives practically every day," he said on social media.
"But a response is needed — Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences."
Last week, Carney told reporters his message to Vladimir Putin will be straight forward if the Russian president attends this year's G20 summit in Miami.

"The message will be simple: 'Get out of Ukraine, give back all of Ukraine to Ukraine, end this war which is killing more than 30,000 of your people every single month,' and I'd leave it at that to be honest."
Carney's message to Putin: 'End this war'
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah Petz is a Toronto-based senior writer with the CBC News live pages team. Born and raised in Manitoba, her career has taken her across three provinces, multiple cities and to northern Uganda.

articles.title: Apple's new iPhone Duo costs more in Canada, but not because of tariffs

image.caption: The iPhone Duo on display on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif., on Wednesday. The phone is retailing for a starting price of $2,999 in Canada. (Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·New

Apple's new foldable iPhone Duo is retailing for prices starting from $2,999 in Canada, before tax. In the U.S., prices start at $1,999 US, which works out as $2,760 — meaning Canadians will have to pay almost 10 per cent more for the cheapest version.
Starting price for foldable phone, revealed on Wednesday, is almost 10% more than in the U.S.
Canadians are used to seeing higher prices than what our neighbours in the U.S., but the price gap for the latest iPhone has caused some double takes.
The iPhone Duo, Apple's new foldable phone revealed Wednesday, is retailing for prices ranging from $2,999 to $4,799 in Canada, before tax.
In the U.S., prices start at $1,999 US, which works out as $2,760 — meaning Canadians will have to pay almost 10 per cent more for the cheapest version.
The sticker shock drew jeers and jokes on a Canadian Reddit forum, with one user saying anyone who spends that much on a phone should have to take a financial literacy class.
"You used to be able to buy a car for that amount," another wrote.

items: Apple unveils iPhone Duo, its new folding phone that costs at least $3K

blocks.text: University of Toronto economics professor Joseph Steinberg says the price bump likely signals that Apple recognized the subset of the Canadian population that would buy a "super-premium product" like the Duo is "less price sensitive" relative to American consumers, "and therefore they can get away with jacking up the margin a little bit more."
He notes that it's not unusual for electronics and other products to be more expensive in Canada.
"This one just stands out because of how darn expensive this phone is, I think, more than anything," Steinberg said.
It's not tariffs: profs
Some have speculated that Canada's new retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products would raise iPhone prices, but experts told CBC News that is not a factor in this case.
While the list of U.S. products tariffed at 50 per cent includes smartphones, Steinberg says Canada does not actually import the devices from the U.S. in any meaningful quantity.
Additionally, Canada's tariffs do not apply to the iPhone Duo because the phones are built in China and are therefore treated as a product originating in China and not the U.S., he says.
Canadian consumers already seeing trade war price hikes
"What matters for whether a tariff is applied is where the project originates from, not where it last crossed the border into Canada from," he added.

Canada's counter-tariffs on U.S. products came into effect early Tuesday, prompting Washington to escalate the countries' trade dispute by banning certain goods imported from Canada and introducing more tariffs of its own later that day.
Microchip shortage raising prices
Werner Antweiler, chair in international trade policy at the University of British Columbia, says virtually all electronics Canadians buy come from Asia, and include components made around the world.

He says the reason smartphone prices are rising in general is because of the global microchip shortage caused by the AI boom and the rapid spread of data centres, creating a "crazy demand" that is driving up manufacturing prices.
Antweiler says he's surprised to see Apple specifically raise its prices more for Canadian consumers, though he notes it's not an uncommon practice for U.S. companies.

"Price discrimination is not unusual, and that can be in the magnitude of 10 to 15 per cent, because that is typically what the Canadian market will pay more," he said, adding that's largely because Canada is a smaller market than the U.S.

items: Why a memory chip shortage is wreaking havoc on the consumer electronics industry

blocks.text: CBC News has contacted Apple for comment but has not heard back.
Apple CEO John Ternus led the unveiling of the iPhone Duo on Wednesday, which marked a major change to the company's flagship product in his first event since taking the leadership role.
Pre-orders for the Duo begin on Oct. 17 and the phone will be available Oct. 23.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ontario court records accessed in cybersecurity breach
articles.summary: The personal information of people involved in Ontario's court systems may have been stolen in a cyber attack, according to the chief justices of the province. An online case management system used…

image.caption: The Ontario Court of Appeal in Toronto is one of the province's courts that is affected by a cyber attack related to an online case-management system it uses. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

The personal information of people involved in Ontario's court systems may have been stolen in a cyber attack, according to the chief justices of the province. An online case management system used by the courts and owned by Thomson Reuters Canada Limited was breached in June.
Personal information in court records may have been compromised
Ontario's chief justices are warning people in the province who have been involved in the court system that their personal information may have been stolen in a cyberattack.

A statement notifying the public about the incident was posted online on Sept. 2, by Ontario Chief Justice Michael H. Tulloch, along with Patrick J. Boucher, chief justice of the Ontario Superior Court, and Sharon M. Nicklas, chief justice of the Ontario Court of Justice.
It says the breach involved an online case-management platform called C-Track, which is owned by Thomson Reuters Canada Limited.
The Court of Appeal for Ontario, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and the Ontario Court of Justice all use C-Track to store and manage court documents and records, according to the notice.

The company detected "unauthorized activity" within one of its cloud environments on June 30. It contacted law enforcement and began its own investigation, which determined that the breach started months earlier, in March, and that court records related to the Court of Appeal for Ontario, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice and the Ontario Court of Justice were obtained by "an unauthorized party."
The company notes that data from the courts was affected but the incident was not caused by the courts' networks or data security.
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter
Sealed information may have been accessed
"Certain confidential, redacted or sealed information may have been impacted for certain affected courts," the company says on a website it has launched about the incident.

Names and other personal information were potentially accessed, it says, but it doesn't specify what kind of personal information or how many records were accessed. It also doesn't indicate how far back the records go.
Additional cybersecurity measures are now in place to better protect C-Track systems and data, the company said.
"Our products and services remain fully operational and are safe to continue to use," the company said in a statement provided to CBC News.
A spokesperson for the company was not available for an interview.

items: Eastlink says data breach affects 75,000 customers
Personal information stolen in data breach last year at Autism Services of Saskatoon

blocks.text: In addition to the website, a call centre is operating to take inquiries, and credit monitoring is being offered to affected individuals.
The company did not provide an estimate of how many Ontarians could be vulnerable because of the cyberattack.
The statement from the chief justices says there's still uncertainty about the exact contents of the files that may have been accessed.

"However, if individuals have been involved in court proceedings or may have been mentioned in court documents, it is possible that some personal information relating to them could have been involved in the incident," the statement said.
Hundreds of ransomware attacks stopped each year, says Canada’s cybersecurity chief
Courts in the U.S. also impacted

The three Ontario courts weren't the only ones impacted by the same cybersecurity incident. Court systems using C-Track in Alabama, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, South Carolina, Tennessee, Ohio, New Hampshire, Wyoming were also involved. The U.S. Virgin Islands was also affected.

A website set up in the U.S. for those affected by the breach notes that some of the personal information that may have been accessed includes driver's licence numbers, social security numbers and medical information.
A statement issued by the New Hampshire Judicial Branch indicates that records in its system affected by the breach cover a period between 2002 and 2015.
The statement from Ontario's chief justices seeks to reassure the public that privacy and security are taken seriously by the courts.
"We remain committed to transparency," the statement reads.

"Throughout this process, our priority is to ensure support for potentially affected individuals, safeguard information entrusted to the courts, and work collaboratively with the government of Ontario to strengthen security measures and reduce the risk of similar incidents in the future."

articles.title: iPhone Duo: Apple unveils its first foldable smartphone
articles.summary: CUPERTINO, United States — Apple unveiled its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, on Wednesday, kicking off the era of new CEO John Ternus. The foldable is a crucial test for Apple, which has not…

blocks.text: CUPERTINO, United States — Apple unveiled its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, on Wednesday, kicking off the era of new CEO John Ternus.
The foldable is a crucial test for Apple, which has not launched a breakout hit since the AirPods 10 years ago.
Wednesday’s event was the first under Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1.

Ternus, 51, joined Apple’s product design team in 2001 and worked his way up to leading the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue.

blocks.caption: New Apple CEO John Ternus, alongside vice president of industrial Molly Anderson, shows off an iPhone Duo during an Apple event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park in Cupertino, California, on September 9, 2026.  (Photo by Karl Mondon / AFP)

blocks.text: The Duo, roughly shaped like a passport when folded, essentially combines the portability of a smartphone with the larger display of a tablet, offering users a bigger screen without carrying a tablet-sized device.
The product has a full external display when closed, a larger internal display when open, and multiple camera lenses.
The Cupertino-based company said it had reduced the visible crease in the middle of the screen — one of the main criticisms leveled at foldables.
It is priced starting at $1,999, slightly more than Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8.
Apple also announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, priced at $1,199 and $1,299 respectively, or $100 more than the iPhone 17 lineup at launch last year.
They will come with an improved camera that allows users to adjust the lens aperture.
Notably, Apple did not announce a cheaper base version of its iPhone, presumably called the iPhone 18, which could indicate it will launch at a later date.

blocks.caption: An attendee takes a selfie with the new foldable iPhone Duo, displayed during an Apple event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park in Cupertino, California, on September 9, 2026. (Photo by Karl Mondon / AFP)

blocks.text: Customers in the United States will be able to pay for new phones, iPads, Macs and Apple Watches in monthly installments through Apple Upgrade, a leasing program offered with the buy-now-pay-later giant Klarna.
For the newest lineup of iPhones, a lease through Apple Upgrade works out to around $50 a month and up.
In late June, the company raised the prices of its Macs and iPads, citing the impact of component shortages caused by the boom in AI, and then warned in July that smartphones would follow.
Seven years later
Chinese competitors released their latest foldable products ahead of the Duo’s unveiling.
On Monday, Huawei unveiled its three-panel Mate XT 2, starting at 19,999 yuan ($2,800), and Xiaomi unveiled its 18 Fold, starting at 10,999 yuan ($1,540).
Samsung launched the industry’s first mainstream foldable smartphone, the Galaxy Fold, in 2019.

Foldable smartphones make up a tiny fraction of the market, at less than 2 percent of global shipments, but Apple is expected to capture about a third of demand with its entry, according to research firm IDC.
“Apple’s foldable iPhone is very likely to shift the competitive dynamics both in China and global markets,” IDC research associate Kiranjeet Kaur told AFP.
The foldable iPhone’s release comes as demand for powerful chips amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom has created a supply chain crunch, pushing prices higher across industries.
As a result, smartphone shipments will decline by more than 16 percent this year while the average cost jumps more than 27 percent, according to IDC.

Apple also announced updated versions of its entry-level AirPods and smart watches, the latter of which will have improved heart-rate sensors that can be paired with an updated Health app launching later this year.

Other rumored devices that did not get mentioned during Wednesday’s event include an updated Apple TV box and HomePod mini speaker, as well as a smart home hub with a 7-inch screen, previously reported by Bloomberg.

articles.title: Release of detainee into Chinatown parking lot prompts anger, calls for reform in Edmonton
articles.summary: Surveillance video showing a former detainee being released from a corrections transport van into the streets of Edmonton’s Chinatown has raised concerns over how Alberta offenders are released into…

image.caption: Security camera footage from a Chinatown in central Edmonton shows a detainee being released from provincial custody into an inner-city parking lot. The footage has renewed public safety concerns in the community. (Yorkton Equity Group)

blocks.text: Surveillance video showing a former detainee being released from a corrections transport van into the streets of Edmonton’s Chinatown has raised concerns over how Alberta offenders are released into the community.

The surveillance footage, recorded on Sept. 3 at 8:30 a.m., shows a white van with a Correctional Services logo pulling into a private parking lot on 105th Avenue between 97th and 98th streets, near the Pacific Mall in Chinatown.
The driver, a uniformed officer, steps out, opens the van’s secured rear doors. The person released from the van is then seen walking away, carrying a stack of documents in his hands.

Karl Miu, vice-chair of the Chinatown Business Association, says the surveillance footage is further evidence that the province’s correctional agencies have been releasing offenders into the central Edmonton neighbourhood without adequate support or supervision.

He has written to Mike Ellis, Alberta’s public safety minister, on behalf of the association, demanding that Alberta tighten its transition protocol for offenders by mandating formal discharge-and-reintegration plans.
Raw video shows provincial corrections van releasing person in parking lot in Edmonton's Chinatown
Miu said he believes Chinatown has become an “unofficial discharge destination” for offenders, and is concerned that the practice undermines public safety in the area.
“The community is furious but also concerned,” Miu said in an interview with CBC News Wednesday. “Chinatown should not become the province's dumping ground.”

items: Downtown Edmonton businesses paying out-of-pocket for security amid public safety concerns

blocks.text: Miu said the concentration of social service agencies in Chinatown, including daytime and overnight shelters, has already created issues of security, poverty and social disorder in the neighbourhood. The video appears to show the officer pointing toward The Hope Mission, located a few blocks away, he said.

Miu is a consultant with the Yorkton Equity Group real estate asset management company, which owns the parking lot. He noted the corrections officer was on private property without permission while making the drop-off.
'Reinforcing expectations' over release policy

In a statement, officials with the Public Safety and Emergency Services ministry said the individual being released had been transported to an area of Edmonton where “various community supports” were located.

“While the intent was to connect the individual with available services, we acknowledge concerns about where the individual was released,” the statement reads. The ministry oversees Alberta Correctional Services.
“We are reinforcing expectations with staff that releases occur at appropriate public locations and not on private property.”

items: In depth: Fighting for change in Chinatown

blocks.text: In the statement, officials said Alberta corrections staff work with incarcerated individuals to develop plans for their release, which includes consideration of transportation needs and available support.
“Both remanded and sentenced individuals are advised to arrange pickup from correctional centres with family, friends or another transportation provider,” the ministry stated.
“When pickup cannot be arranged, centre staff will facilitate transportation based on the individual’s home community, immediate needs and available supports.”

Alberta is responsible for operating correctional centres for both adults and youth who are serving sentences under two years, as well as designated remand centres for those awaiting trial or bail hearings.
Alberta ministry officials did not provide details about the person who was released, including the status of their release, age, or where and why they had been held in custody.

“Due to privacy considerations, we are unable to provide personal information about individuals in custody or under community supervision ... unless that information is already part of the public record or there is a specific legislative authority permitting its release,” officials said.
CBC News has blurred the detainee's identity in the video because the person's identification of and circumstances of his release are not confirmed.
Ellis, the public safety minister, declined an interview request Wednesday. The Alberta Union of Provincial Employees also declined to comment on member involvement in the drop-off.

items: Justin Bone case illustrates gaps in Alberta's social services, lawyers and addictions specialists say

blocks.text: In his letter to the province, Miu said the video demonstrates the urgent need for Alberta to reform how it releases offenders from its correctional facilities.

People being discharged from provincial custody need to be carefully managed, he said, with clear release conditions, confirmed housing placements, detailed mental health and addictions assessments and prolonged follow-up care by case managers.

“Why should Chinatown businesses, residents, workers and visitors experience the consequences of a failed transition plan that was supposed to be managed by the provincial correctional and social-service systems,” Miu wrote in his letter.

items: Police could have arrested man on bail breaches days before Edmonton's Chinatown killings, experts say

blocks.text: A failure in transition planning can have tragic consequences, Miu said.

He said the incident has parallels to the release of Justin Bone, who was taken to Edmonton by the Alberta RCMP in May 2022, in violation of his bail conditions that barred him from being unsupervised in the city.

Bone was arrested three days later, charged in the deaths of two Chinatown residents, Hung Trang and Ban Phuc Hoang. The high-profile homicides stoked safety fears in Chinatown and prompted concerns about the strength of Alberta’s enforcement systems for offenders on release conditions.
'Tossing people out'
David Shepherd, the NDP MLA for Edmonton-City Centre, said his heart dropped when he viewed the security footage.
He said such drop-offs undermine the ongoing efforts of Chinatown residents and business owners to revitalize the neighbourhood in the years since the tragic killings.
The video, he said, demonstrates that there are still concerning gaps in Alberta’s correctional system.

“We really need to see the UCP government step up and make sure that the services and supports are available and that we're working with the correctional system to ensure that we're not just sort of tossing people out."
Chris Hayes, executive director of the John Howard Society of Alberta, said incarcerated individuals face unique challenges after they have served their time.
He said discharging them without basic support and oversight — a systemic issue that is seen across Canada — often guarantees their failure to safely reintegrate.
“If we just punt someone out of a van into downtown Edmonton without supports, the research shows that the odds of their success are almost zero.”
In an interview Wednesday, Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said the footage reinforces an ongoing issue in the city that demands clear solutions from both the provincial and federal governments.

He said Edmonton is surrounded by a large number of correctional facilities and that concentration requires stronger policies to ensure that there is a plan in place for every person who is discharged from custody into the capital region.

“To see that clearly on video is a reminder that this is an issue that demands a clear set of solutions," Knack said. "Being dropped in a parking lot, even if there was a plan to go somewhere else, doesn't feel like a great solution.”

articles.title: Power outages: CERA seeks probe into 'recurring' plant shutdowns
articles.summary: MANDAUE CITY, Cebu — The recurring unexplained outages affecting Cebu and other parts of the Visayas Grid are pushing the region to the “brink of collapse.” Nathaniel Chua, lead…

blocks.text: MANDAUE CITY, Cebu — The recurring unexplained outages affecting Cebu and other parts of the Visayas Grid are pushing the region to the “brink of collapse.”
Nathaniel Chua, lead convenor of the Cebu Electricity Rights Advocates (CERA), said the power crisis currently affecting the region is the result of a “dual failure” in generation and transmission.

Chua said there is now a need to investigate the recurring power outages, which have severely affected residents and businesses in the area, as well as the country’s power grid infrastructure as a whole.
“It is completely unacceptable that our major power plants are suddenly ‘conking out’ at the exact same time, plunging Cebu’s households and businesses into deep uncertainty,” Chua said.

“We are demanding an immediate congressional inquiry and a strict audit by the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). Consumers deserve to know why these multibillion-peso facilities are failing when we need them the most. Are these genuine technical failures, or is there a lack of proper maintenance and foresight by the generation companies?” he added.
Critical baseload supply
Quoting data from the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP), Chua said the Visayas grid had already endured at least 73 consecutive days of yellow and red alerts.
On Wednesday, September 9, the Visayas grid was placed under red alert from 1 p.m. to 10 p.m., followed by a yellow alert from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m.
Available capacity for the day stood at 2,124 megawatts, while peak demand reached 2,555 megawatts, resulting in a 431-megawatt shortfall.

The situation was attributed to the unavailability of major coal-fired power plants, including Therma Visayas Inc. (TVI) Unit 1 and Panay Energy Development Corporation (PEDC) Unit 3, as well as the outage of TVI Unit 2 and limited power imports from the Mindanao grid.
Congressional inquiry

In an advisory, NGCP said 11 power plants were on forced outage as of September. Four plants had been on forced outage since August 2026, one since July, two since June, seven since May, three since 2025, two since 2024, two since 2023, and one since 2021.
Moreover, 13 power plants were operating at derated capacities. In total, around 982.6 megawatts of power capacity remained unavailable to the grid.
Infrastructure failure

Beyond the failing power plants, CERA also highlighted a critical infrastructure problem exacerbating the crisis: a glaring bottleneck in the country’s transmission network connecting the major island grids.

At present, the Mindanao-Visayas Interconnection Project (MVIP) allows up to 450 MW of power to be shared between the two southern island regions, a capacity that the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) has said could be expanded to 900 MW.
In contrast, the older Luzon-Visayas HVDC interconnection has a maximum transfer capacity of only 440 MW.

“NGCP itself has acknowledged this bottleneck, confirming it is undertaking an upgrade of the Luzon-Visayas HVDC line that would double its transfer capacity from 440 MW to 880 MW — an admission that the current link is inadequate for a grid this size,” he said.
Massive Inequity

Chua added that while the Visayas grid suffered from supply shortage, “the Luzon grid has generally maintained normal conditions with far more generating capacity in reserve, at times posting available capacity well in excess of 14,000 MW against system peak demand of around of close to 10,000 MW— leaving more than 3,000 MW of reserve capacity that could not be fully transmitted south because of the constrained interconnection.”
“This is a tragic irony and a massive inequity,” Chua explained.

“We expect the Visayas and Mindanao to bear the brunt of the crisis and help each other with their 450 MW interconnection. Meanwhile, Luzon, which holds the vast majority of the country’s generating capacity and regularly carries thousands of megawatts in reserve, can only share a fraction of that to alleviate supply problems in the South,” Chua said.

Meanwhile, CERA is calling on the national government and NGCP to fast-track the planned upgrade of the Luzon-Visayas interconnection from 440 MW to 880 MW, and to explore further capacity expansion beyond that, so that excess power from the north can flow to the Visayas and Mindanao grids during emergencies without delay.

“Cebuanos are paying a premium for electricity, and in return, we are given months of red alerts and excuses,” Chua added. “We need full accountability from the power plants, and we need our transmission infrastructure reviewed and modernized immediately. Our economy and our daily lives can no longer afford these structural failures.”

articles.title: UK chancellor urged to remove £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ prompting parents to cut work hours
articles.summary:
Critics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlement

John Healey has been urged to fix the £100,000 childcare…

blocks.text: John Healey has been urged to fix the £100,000 childcare “cliff edge”, that means some higher-paid employees cut back on work to avoid losing their entitlement.

Since the latest expansion of taxpayer-funded childcare in 2024, families with young children in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care - or none at all, if one of them cross that threshold.

In a report, researchers from the Centre for Tax Reform (CenTax) said that, by the end of this parliament in 2030, the average parent crossing this “cliff edge”, will have to earn £124,000, to be no worse off after losing their free childcare.
Arun Advani, director of CenTax, said: “Our analysis shows the childcare cliff edge stands to grow dramatically by the end of this parliament, but there are solutions available to the government.”

The researchers find that “bunching” of incomes just below the threshold suggests that even in 2022 – the latest year for which data is available – about 1,000 families were artificially suppressing their earnings to avoid falling foul of the threshold. That could rise to almost 12,000 by the end of this parliament.

The thinktank, based at Warwick University, also suggested the policy may be incentivising some mothers to drop out of work. Below the £100,000 threshold, 6% of lower-paid partners – usually the mother – are out of work; but above the threshold that rises to 9%.

“The jump in non-working mothers at the point where their partner exceeds £100,000 income suggests the loss of childcare entitlement as a cause, with possible long-term consequences for those mothers’ earnings,” the report said.

CenTax also criticised the fact that the threshold is based on how much parents expect to earn in the year ahead – pointing out that some families appear to be claiming it, despite eventually earning more than £100,000.
It proposes several potential solutions. Restricting free childcare to 15 hours to families above the £100,000 threshold, instead of withdrawing it altogether, would cost £210m by 2030, it said.
Gradually tapering away the entitlement at 28p for each £1 earned above the threshold would be revenue neutral, but less problematic for parents, it adds.
Healey is set to deliver his first budget on 28 October, against a backdrop of renewed fears about higher inflation and febrile global bond markets.
after newsletter promotion

Analysts believe higher than expected interest rates on the Treasury’s debt are likely to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom that Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves built up against the government’s fiscal rules.

In his first major speech in Coventry on Monday, Healey promised to put growth at the heart of his approach; but also warned that Labour must “be honest” about the constraints on public spending in the years ahead.

Since taking over as Labour leader in July, Andy Burnham has announced a VAT cut on electricity bills and capped bus fares; but Healey has also suggested the government is keen to do more to give hard-pressed consumers a “breathing space”.

articles.title: Teachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in school
articles.summary:
School staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisis

Teachers have so little belief in the importance of pupils’ full school…

blocks.text: Teachers have so little belief in the importance of pupils’ full school attendance that they would take their own children on term time holidays if they could, staff have told a three-year research programme.

Frontline staff do not believe the school system is set up to deal with an ongoing attendance crisis in England and Wales, where nearly one in five children are now missing at least 10% of school, according to a report based on in-depth conversations with teachers.

Despite a hardline approach from schools to tackle the crisis, evidence from focus groups containing teachers from schools in low-income areas suggests many share the same scepticism as parents and pupils about the efficiency of holiday fines, according to the report by youth charity Impetus and policy and polling research firm Public First.
“If I wasn’t a teacher, I would take my daughter out of school and take her on holiday because it would be cheaper,” said one teacher.
Another noted: “If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school in January.”

The report comes as the children’s commissioner warned of tens of thousands of hidden Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), with analysis suggesting that an estimated 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds enrolled in colleges in England are attending less than half the time.

Rachel de Souza warned that the number of Neets is almost twice as large as official figures indicate, according to a new analysis of 262 of England’s 290 college groups, which are not included in Department for Education attendance figures.

“We have a blind spot: hidden Neets slipping through the cracks,” she said. “Young people with all the negative impacts of not being in employment, education or training, but with none of the targeted interventions.”
Researchers compiling the report, A Crisis of Disengagement, spoke to 62 secondary school staff from schools where more than 25% of pupils were eligible for free school meals.
They spoke of the work of chasing pupils’ attendance as “relentless” and expressed the view that an occasional holiday or minor absence was less worrying than sustained disengagement.
While some staff saw fines as a necessary tool, many believed they damage trust and undermine the relational work needed to support pupils and families to re-engage with school.
“We’ll send a penalty notice out and then we’ve really annoyed that parent,” said one senior leader. “We’ve just broken a relationship between a family that we want to get into school.”

A record 492,825 penalty notices for unauthorised absences were issued to parents in England in 2024-25, a sharp rise from pre-Covid levels. Researchers have previously warned of a “seismic shift” in attitudes to attendance since the pandemic, with concern that some parents no longer believe children needed to be in school full-time. The absence rate for pupils in England in 2025-26 was 6.93%, significantly above the 2018-19 pre-Covid level of 4.7%

Teachers and senior leaders in schools also argued that gaps in mental health support for struggling students, unmet special educational needs and a paucity of social workers was making their jobs more difficult with schools seen as “the one-stop shop for everything”.

“We’ve got children who should have specialist provision, and they’re in our building every day,” said one senior leader. “We also need external agencies such as CAMHS [Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services] and social workers to have the right capacity and not turn us down.”
Staff also told researchers the most effective interventions were also the hardest – including building relationships, mentoring and home visits.
“I think it takes up a lot of adult hours,” she said. “If you looked proportionally at how time was broken down, attendance is very, very time consuming.”
Susannah Hardyman, CEO of Impetus, said teachers could not solve the attendance crisis alone.

“We now know that not only are pupils, families and teachers unconvinced that every day in school matters, but what we are facing is a wider crisis of disengagement driven by pressures often outside the control of school staff,” she said.

articles.title: 'Negative na': Small Manila businesses cut staff, take loans over steep garbage fees
articles.summary: One to two trash bags a day, P60,000 garbage bill: Manila businesses are crying foul over new garbage fees.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Small business owners in Manila are reeling from a sharp increase in garbage collection fees imposed during this year's business permit renewal.

Already struggling with operating costs, business owners interviewed by Philstar.com said the higher fees have pushed their finances further into the red, forcing some to cut staff or take out loans. At least one establishment was also ordered closed by the Manila local government over unpaid permit-related fees.
For Vince Canlas, owner of El Latte Cafe on Taft Avenue, the new fees have made the reality of doing business in Manila an uphill battle.
Originally starting as a milk tea shop in Olongapo, the business relocated to Manila to tap into the large student market near major universities.
The 100-square-meter cafe has just five employees. So when he renewed the permit, he was shocked at what he was asked to pay.
"Nagulat kami sa garbage fee. Na sobrang laki. Nakakagulat lang talaga. Hindi namin in-expect na mangyayari pala sa amin," Canlas told Philstar.com in an interview.
(We were taken aback by how high the garbage fee was. It was really surprising. We never expected this would happen to us.)
Canlas said the cafe incurred nearly P107,000 in fees for its business permit renewal. Around P60,000 was for garbage collection, including interest due to late payment.
"Sabi ko manager ko, 'Sir, gaano ba karami ang tinatapon natin daily?' Sabi niya, 'Boss, ano lang 'to, nasa one to two bags lang.' Sobrang baba so hindi talaga makatarungan ang P60,000," Canlas said.
(I asked my manager how much garbage we generate daily, and he said it was only around one or two bags. Given how little waste we produce, a P60,000 garbage fee is simply unreasonable.)
To survive, Canlas reduced his employees' working days, resulting in lower take-home pay.
"Wala kaming choice kasi wala naman kaming ibang pwedeng i-cut na ano eh. Para lang mabawasan 'yung alam mo 'yun, 'yung gastusin eh," Canlas said.
(We had no choice because there really wasn't anything else we could cut. We just needed to bring down our expenses.)
Making things worse, the Manila local government ordered the closure of his cafe on September 1 after he struggled to settle the fees.
To save the cafe, Canlas took out a new loan to pay the nearly P107,000 assessment on the same day.
After settling the amount, howver, Canlas said the city still required them to pay another P6,200 in penalties before they were allowed to reopen.
"Baka tapusin na lang itong year na 'to. Isara na lang namin ang cafe; wala na talaga eh, negative na dahil sa mga bills," Canlas said.
(We might just finish out this year and shut down the cafe. We really have no choice left. We're already operating at a loss because of all these bills.)
"Grabe, nakaka-iyak sa Manila. Parang tingin nila pinupulot namin ang pera," he added.
Reduced staff
Outdoor seating next to food stalls at Manila's Fusion Alley in Sampaloc as seen in September 2026.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
For Kriska Castillejos, owner of a food stall near Manila's Fusion Alley in Sampaloc, the financial pressure meant letting go of nine of her 15 employees.
Like other business owners interviewed by Philstar.com, Castillejos said her stall suffered financially because of what she described as a sudden spike in costs of business in the city.
For the previous year, she paid about P14,000 in renewal fees. In 2026, the amount ballooned to P64,000.
"Malaki 'yung ano niya, 'yung impact niya talaga. Lalo na kami maliliit, nagpapasahod kami ng tao," Castillejos said in a Philstar.com interview.
(It really has a huge impact, especially on small business owners like us who have employees to pay.)
The ordinance
In January 2026, the Manila local government began implementing revised garbage collection fees under Ordinance 9151, with some commercial rates rising to 12 times their previous levels.
Before the revised schedule, Manila followed the garbage collection rates under its 2013 Omnibus Revenue Code.
For instance, the quarterly garbage fee for the main office of a commercial bank was previously P1,250, while each branch was charged P225.
Under the revised schedule, both a commercial bank's main office and each branch are charged P15,000 per quarter.
Public eating places with an aggregate area of 100 to less than 200 square meters, meanwhile, are now charged P16,800 per quarter.
Call for fairer fees
Business owners urged Manila Mayor Isko Moreno Domagoso to reconsider the steep increases.
Canlas said he does not hold any personal animosity toward the local government but believes its current policies are putting more pressure on small enterprises.
"Sana ma-hear kami na magiging balance lang sa lahat. May proyekto para sa mahirap, may proyekto para sa mga small business owners," Canlas said.
(I hope we are heard and that there will be balance for everyone, with projects for the poor as well as projects for small business owners.)

"Hindi naman namin hinihiling na malaki ang bumalik sa amin. Ang gusto lang talaga namin makapag-operate nang wala kaming iniisip na, hala, may bayarin malaking ganito. Mabubuhay, makakapag-operate pa ba tayo para sa mga employees natin?" he added.
(We aren't asking for huge returns. All we really want is to operate without constantly worrying about massive bills and wondering whether we can survive and continue operating for our employees.)

Castillejos, meanwhile, urged the city hall to focus on strict waste segregation, penalties for littering and investments in recycling rather than imposing increasingly heavy fees on already struggling businesses.
"Kasi talagang may basura naman tayo eh. Kailangan nating magbayad para sa ika-uunlad din natin. Ang ano ko lang is dapat hindi sobrang taas," Castillejos said.
(We recognize that we generate waste and need to pay our share. My only point is that the fee should not be this high.)
Comparison with other cities
Under Manila's revised schedule, public eating places with an aggregate area of 100 to less than 200 square meters are assessed a quarterly garbage fee of P16,800, or P67,200 annually.
The amount is notably higher than waste collection fees described by other local governments in responses to Philstar.com:

items: San Juan City: Annual garbage fees range from P200 to P15,000 depending on the size and type of business and are collected during the application or renewal of business permits, according to San Juan Mayor Francis Zamora.

Marikina City: Restaurants are charged annual garbage fees of around P3,000 to P5,000, while catering services are charged P12,000 per year. Rates for smaller establishments vary depending on their classification.
Las Piñas: Businesses are charged annual fees ranging from P3,000 to P20,000.
Pasig City: Restaurants and cafes are charged P5 per square meter monthly. For a 100-square-meter cafe, this amounts to P500 a month, or P6,000 annually.
Navotas City: The Assessment Department of Business Permits and Licensing told Philstar.com that the city collects P1,500 to P7,500 as garbage disposal fees for food businesses' annual payments.

blocks.text: What did the Manila LGU say?
Philstar.com has reached out to the Manila Public Information Office for comment but has yet to receive a response as of press time.
In a January statement, the Manila local government defended Ordinance No. 9151 as "lawful and constitutionally sound."

City officials said an earlier Supreme Court ruling involving Quezon City's garbage fees did not apply to Manila's ordinance because the city's revised charges were imposed on businesses as regulatory fees rather than as taxes.

"In contrast, he said, Manila's revised garbage collection fees apply exclusively to business establishments and are imposed as regulatory fees, not taxes, consistent with jurisprudence recognizing the validity of cost-based garbage charges," the Manila LGU's January statement read.

City Legal Officer Luch Gempis Jr. said the rates had not been updated since 2013 despite increases in commercial waste volumes and garbage hauling costs, particularly after Manila was advised to redirect its waste to the New San Mateo Sanitary Landfill in Rizal.
City Treasurer Paul Vega similarly said the revised rates were intended to narrow the gap between the cost of garbage collection and the revenue generated from the fees.

Bureau of Permits Director Levi Facundo, meanwhile, said fee assessments are automatically generated based on the schedules under the ordinance and advised business owners with billing concerns to coordinate with the appropriate city departments.
Supreme Court junks plea
The implementation of the garbage fee ordinance was challenged before the Supreme Court on February 5, 2026.

The petition was filed by Las Piñas-based senior high school teacher John Barry Tayam, who invoked the "doctrine of transcendental importance" and sought a temporary restraining order against the implementation of the ordinance.
In a February 25 resolution, however, the Supreme Court dismissed the petition, ruling that Tayam lacked legal standing for not being a Manila resident.
It also ruled that the petitioner violated the doctrine of hierarchy of courts by filing the case directly with the high tribunal. — with additional reporting by Ella Mae Soriano

articles.title: What will Trump's retaliatory tariffs do to Canada’s economy big picture? Not that much, economists predict
articles.summary: With some tariffs added and others removed, economists predict that big picture the changes will break even. But certain industries will still be hit hard, they say, and the tit-for-tat will weigh on…

image.caption: Economists say this week's retaliation in the trade war will hurt some sectors and dent business confidence, but the sheer impact on the economy will be negligible. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

With some tariffs added and others removed, economists predict that big picture the changes will break even. But certain industries will still be hit hard, they say, and the tit-for-tat will weigh on business owners' confidence.
Real hit will be indirect, economists warn — as some businesses likely to feel relief, others 'horrified'
The White House fired another shot in the Canada-U.S. trade war this week, banning outright the imports of Canadian dairy, motorcycles and some alcohol products.
But how much will those bans, along with fresh 50 per cent tariffs on a slate of other products, actually impact the Canadian economy?
Not all that much, say economists who’ve run the numbers. But that doesn't mean it won't hurt certain industries — and it certainly won't give business owners any peace of mind.

On Tuesday night, the White House retaliated against Canada's counter-tariffs with the bans and the addition of 50 per cent tariffs to items including mattresses and some paper products. American officials also dropped tariffs on others, such as toilet paper, cement and sugar.

But according to one analysis from Derek Holt, vice president and head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, the new tariffs will apply to an estimated $3 billion worth of Canadian goods, while the removed tariffs apply to about $2 billion worth — making the difference marginal, given Canada exported more than $527 billion worth of goods to the U.S. in 2025.

items: Trump banning import of Canadian booze, motorcycles, other goods into U.S.

blocks.text: The bans on alcohol, dairy and motorcycles will also be negligible, Holt adds, as Canada sends very little dairy and few motorcycles south of the border. Alcohol exports are a bit higher than the other categories, with $550 million worth sent to the U.S. last year, according to his analysis, but the export bans would still only impact $700 million worth of Canadian exports to the U.S.
"These actions are face saving by the U.S. administration, not substantive in nature and that’s a positive," Holt said in a note to investors on Wednesday.
How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians?

He says the rising cost of oil — which soared past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday due to escalating tensions in the Middle East — poses a greater economic risk than the new U.S. measures.

At BMO, chief economist Doug Porter agrees. His team puts the value of newly tariffed items and those taken off the list both at about $2 billion, putting the country "in the same spot" as it was before the announcement.
But where the tariffs do hit, in certain industries or parts of the country, they will still hurt business owners badly, Porter told CBC News.

items: Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about shopping in the age of the Canada-U.S. trade dispute? Send us your questions before our Sept. 12 show.

blocks.text: "It's extremely negative for the new industries and products that were selected, but of course, some pretty important ones were taken off the list," he said.
"So there are going to be some relieved industries today and some horrified."
50% tariffs already an effective ban

For makers of Canadian booze, further escalation isn't a positive sign. Cal Bricker, CEO of Spirits Canada, says Canada exports much of the alcohol it makes to the U.S., making the continued targeting of his industry a concern.
U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says
But because many alcohol products already faced 50 per cent tariffs, upping the ante to a ban might not make a material difference to many booze producers.
Matt Johnston of craft brewer Collective Arts in Hamilton, Ont., says he wouldn't have been able to send any more of his beer south at a 50 per cent rate anyway.
"The reality is that once you add 50 per cent tariffs, it becomes extremely difficult to try and sell on the market.”

He already sent months worth of product to the U.S. before the new tariffs came into effect a few weeks ago, in hopes a deal could be reached before supplies ran out. Now, the plan is to grow the business within Canada and other international markets to make up for the loss of U.S. sales, where a fifth of their business used to come from.
"The world's a big place and we can look elsewhere," Johnston said.

As with alcohol, many of the banned items were already facing 50 per cent tariffs, RBC economist Nathan Janzen points out, which would have effectively kept them out of the U.S. market, meaning the impact of the ban will be relatively small.
Real hit will be indirect
Even if the impact will be small by the numbers, Tu Nguyen, an economist at accounting firm RSM Canada, says the escalation is still very real in terms of the message it sends to business owners.

While the U.S. has historically increased the tariff percentages in order to turn up the heat on Canada, Nguyen says an all-out ban signals a departure from that strategy. She says the real hit from the escalating retaliation will be indirect — the tit for tat denting business confidence.
"A lot of these tariffs, they sound really big … but they don't hit the economy nearly as badly as one would think," Nguyen said.
“The bigger hit, I would say … comes from uncertainty.”

And unlike in the past, when the U.S. gave many weeks or months of lead time before tariffs went into effect, some of the newly announced measures will come into force as soon as next week. Nguyen says this gives businesses less time to prepare or pivot to new markets, and introduces another worry for business owners on both sides of the border.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Shawn Benjamin

articles.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
articles.summary: Google has announced a plan to expand AI data centers and buy massive amounts of nuclear energy. Finland's security services have warned of there are risks, but the right-wing government says the…

image.caption: Google has signed a deal to purchase half of the energy produced at the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant over the next 22 yearsImage: Anne Kauranen/REUTERS

blocks.text: US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.
Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.

Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.
Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.
Why communities are fighting AI data centers
Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs

In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.
The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."
Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland ⁠remains sufficient and that prices remain under ​control."
The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."

"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.
Resources under pressure
Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk

Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.
Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.
"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," ‌said Google President and ​Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."

Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.
Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.

Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.

SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.

SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.
AI under pressure: scams, security and sustainability

articles.title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
articles.summary:
Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking

The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which

blocks.text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.
Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.

“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.

The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.

Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.

In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.
During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.

On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.

Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel Noboa  Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.

During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government.
During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.

Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.
